Katalog Berita (Halaman 56/58)

#487. The 8 best headphones of 2026: We tested the top contenders from Sony, Apple, Bose, and Beats

In 2026, a pair of headphones or earbuds is pretty much non-optional. That's why there are hundreds of different headphones shapes, sizes, styles, colors, and, of course, prices. These days, you can grab a random pair off the digital shelf without too much research and find that they do the job just fine. However, if you're tired of settling for "just fine," then it's worth investing in the best headphones available.

But be warned: The latest generation of flagship noise-cancelling headphones from the likes of Apple, Sony, and Bose will set you back $450 or more, though we have options to recommend for every price range.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

To help you find the best pair of headphones possible, our experts test headphones year-round, from popular models to new releases to budget picks (you can learn more about our detailed testing standards below). The result of that vetting is this guide, which we keep updated regularly to give you the most accurate and current purchasing information possible. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Read our full review of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones.

Audiophiles and custom equalizer fans: After three years, Sony's flagship wireless headphones finally got an update. If you love Sony headphones and have an old pair of XM4s, then we can definitely recommend an upgrade. However, if you just purchased a pair of XM5s, then it might be harder to justify an instant upgrade. That said, the active noise cancellation is better than ever, and there are noticeable improvements to audio quality (even if they lose out by a smidge to the latest Technics AZ100 earbuds). Besides music lovers, travelers will also appreciate the new Sony cans, as they fold up and come with an improved travel case.

Mashable's Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth reviewed the XM6 headphones ahead of their launch, and he was impressed with the overall quality. As Werth wrote in his review, "The new Sony headphones offer impressive audio quality, and they definitely improve on the XM5 models. The active noise cancellation is particularly phenomenal...I really appreciated the overall balance, depth, and quality of the audio. For the XM6, Sony audio engineers worked with music mastering engineers here in the United States, and the results are clear when you listen to music. Like all headphone reviewers, I have a dedicated playlist for testing new audio products, and I found that vocal-heavy tracks sound particularly great, with noticeable improvements over the XM5s."

Sony introduced (or, rather, brought back) a major design change for the XM6 headphones — they fold up for easier storage. They're definitely more compact and easier to travel with compared to the previous-gen model. The overall design looks similar, so if you're a fan of the Sony aesthetic, you'll still appreciate how they look.

We do wish there had been slightly bigger improvements after a three-year wait, and the battery life (30 hours with ANC engaged) is the same as the XM5 model, which we also loved. These headphones did arrive with a higher sticker price, so if you can't quite swing the $448 price tag, look for the excellent XM5 headphones on sale.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen).

Those who want the best of the best: For anyone who's yet to buy into the Bose QuietComfort Ultra line, but wants noise-cancelling headphones that can easily handle long hours of wear, there's no better choice than the second generation Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones.

The best noise-cancelling headphones aren't much use if they squeeze your head too tight or prevent you from wearing accessories like earrings or glasses comfortably. In other words, comfort is key — we were big fans of Bose's first gen QC Ultra headphones for exactly this reason.

With the second generation of the headphones, Bose makes minor improvements to the soundscape, noise-cancelling, and somehow the wear. They also fixed other bugs that detracted from the otherwise premium experience of using the QC Ultras.

As a first step, Bose upped the battery life from 24 to 30 hours per charge with ANC. They also added options for wired playback with the USB-C cable (which can simultaneously charge the headphones) or the auxiliary cable for passive playback (which wasn't available on the first gen headphones). In tandem with the battery life, these headphones become much stronger contenders for travel.

For day-to-day use, Bose's noise cancelling remains as solid as ever (though Sony's XM6s are ever so slightly more adept at handling high pitched frequencies), while offering an easy adjustment on 10 different levels of ANC via the companion app. As for the listening experience, the immersive audio remains as lackluster as it did on the first gen, but the overall sound profile came through richer and more robust when we compared the headphones side by side. Bose also added quality of life adjustments like better wear detection, and a lay flat mode that puts the headphones into a low power mode when they're placed face down. Overall, it's hard to beat this blend of sound quality, ANC, and comfort, making the second iteration of the QC Ultras one of our top picks for headphones.

Value fiends: If you don't particularly care to have the most premium pair of headphones on the market (or care to spend several hundred dollars on them), the JLab JBuds Lux ANC headphones are the best budget headphones available. They have functional ANC, decent comfort, great sound balance, and a killer battery life, all with a design that doesn't feel cheap.

At their regular sale price of around $50, these are about a ninth the price of the latest Sony headphones, and a seventh of the price of the Bose QuietComfort headphones, which feel like these headphones' premium analogue.

With budget headphones, it's good to understand what you're trading off from the jump. In the case of these JLab headphones, the ANC will dampen a good amount of environmental sound, from talking coworkers to loud fans, but it won't completely silence the world around you. The app can lag some (we had to exit out of it a few times during testing when it froze), and the fit of these headphones might not be for everyone. For one of our testers, these headphones squeezed their head more than usual (though some users on Reddit called these the most comfortable headphones they've tried). Regardless of the fit, you're likely to hear some creaking from time to time when you move your head around.

At $80, these are all cons that may not be ideal, but are fair for the price point. At these headphones' frequent sale prices that hover in the $50 to $55 range, these cons are even easier to swallow, especially when you consider how these headphones actually sound.

To be clear, you'll likely need to play around with the EQ some to find your perfect settings — we found the first preset to be on the bass-heavy end. Once you do, it's impressive the way these headphones can balance a song. Every part of Panic! At The Disco's "Northern Downpour" shone through, from the vocals, lead guitar, bass, and piano. For budget headphones, we might expect some muddying through these elements, but the JLab JBuds held up great. If we're being nitpicky, The Beatles' "In My Life" came through somewhat dimmer sounding than expected, but not necessarily muddy.

Beyond the sound signature, these headphones have a reasonable amount of customization with the app, especially for their price point. You can adjust the button commands on one of the three on-ear buttons, adjust the ANC intensity with a slider in the app, and create your own custom EQ settings. Multipoint pairing is available, as are spatial audio, music, and movie modes.

Check out our full guide to the best Sony headphones.

Students, casual users, and anyone looking for great sound on the cheap: The new price of entry for flagship noise-cancelling headphones? A cool $450, at least. So, if you're looking for wireless headphones with true active noise cancellation but don't want to spend more than $100, then go with Sony's mid-range noise-cancellers. They have Sony's signature sound (and signature all-plastic design, sadly), and you can almost always find them on sale for under $100 at Amazon and other retailers.

These headphones perform much better than you'd expect a pair of $100 cans to perform. They have surprisingly impressive ANC and multipoint pairing, as well as impressive sound — hardly a surprise with a pair of Sony headphones.

As our reviewer Alex Bracetti wrote, "The WH-CH720 employs 30mm drivers and exclusive brand technologies to broaden sound performance. Expect a vibrant mix of impactful bass with striking mids and highs. Turning on DSEE raises fidelity on poor-quality recordings, which many luxury headphones can’t do. You can tweak the sound to your liking via the EQ, though the headphones sound great on their default setting."

Read our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

Folks too busy to charge their devices: If you're just a little too familiar with the low battery sound on your headphones, the absurdly long battery life on the Nothing Headphone (a) gets you as close as you can to a guarantee that you'll hear it as little as possible. Plus, it has a standout retro design.

Picking the headphones with the best battery life isn't a terribly complex process. That said, it isn't just about picking the pair that can pack the most hours — it's about finding the headphones with the best combination of value, overall performance, and, of course, battery life.

Our standard before was set at 60 hours, which is a great deal higher than the 30 hours you'll find on the Bose and Sony headphones on this list. The Nothing Headphone (a) absolutely blows that standard out of the water, offering 75 hours per charge with ANC on, and 135 hours without.

They check the remaining boxes at $199, which, while not dirt cheap, is a fair deal cheaper than most $400+ flagship models. The sound quality is clear and robust, the noise cancellation will get the job done (if not flawlessly), and the on-ear controls are truly a thing of perfection. During testing, we almost never reached for our devices when adjusting settings because the on-ear controls made it so easy not to. Rounding out the experience is a companion app that's easy to navigate, with features like an eight-band equalizer designed to make your music sound just to your liking.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Travelers, students, and anyone blending comfort and value: A lot about our most comfortable headphones pick sounds great, but you're caught up on the price point — understandable. Though a truly excellent, well-rounded headphones experience often comes with a higher price point, Bose's latest headphones — the second generation QuietComforts — prove that investment doesn't need to exceed $400 (for now).

If you're looking for extreme comfort, quality ANC, warm and balanced sound, and a few extras without totally breaking the bank, these are your headphones.

These aren't perfect headphones. The sound profile isn't the most customizable with a three-band equalizer, there's no truly passive playback with the wired connections, the noise cancellation will get staticky during a plane takeoff, and the battery life leans on the low side at 24 hours (finding 30 hours or up isn't too hard these days on a pair of over-ear headphones).

All this to say, these aren't technically perfect headphones, but those cons pale in comparison to their pros. At $359, these headphones are nearly $100 cheaper than the Bose QC Ultra 2 headphones, but offer many of the same features. For starters, the comfort and noise cancellation are nearly on par with the significantly more expensive headphones, which is to say it's very, very good — like easily wearable for a full day of travel. The tactile controls are intuitive and functional, the colorways are varied and unique while remaining appealing, and there's an Immersive Audio listening mode for changing up how you hear your music.

In a time when most tech prices are rising, it's refreshing to see a brand release a pair of headphones that strive for ultra-premium performance, while sticking to a more mildly premium price point.

Read our original review of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones, or see how they compare to the new XM6 headphones.

Last-gen lovers: If you want a premium pair of Sony noise-cancelling headphones but refuse to pay more than $400 for a pair of headphones, we feel you. We also have good news: The XM5 headphones hold up well in 2026, and they're still worth the investment, especially when they're on sale.

Originally released in 2022, the Sony XM5 headphones are still legendary. They had unbeatable ANC and sound for the money, and even in 2026, they sound shockingly good. That's because the new flagship XM6 model only made iterative improvements over these cans. So, now that they go on sale for as little as $248, you just can't write off the older XM5s.

This Mashable Choice product received a 4.7 out of 5 stars in our original review, and even when we recently compared them head-to-head with their successors, they performed incredibly well.

We won't beat around the bush: There's no definitive "best" product here. Sure, elite audio brands put out high-quality products across the board, but even within each of those brands, you'll find different tiers of products. Some will deliver better value, and some will deliver better hardware and active noise cancellation.

All this to say, the best pair of earbuds or headphones largely comes down to personal preference and how you plan to use them. Some listeners swear by over-ear headphones, while others prefer the minimalism of earbuds — one is not necessarily better than the other. Athletes who like to use headphones at the gym will appreciate waterproof materials and the best open earbuds, while frequent fliers will prefer devices with long battery life, comfort, and portability. Finally, music lovers and audiophiles will want to invest in premium features like a custom equalizer, spatial audio, or best-in-class active noise cancellation.

To help you pick your pair, we tested all of the headphones in this guide (and a lot that didn't make the cut). Here, you'll find the top headphones of 2026 for noise cancellation, music, price, and wired connections.

We focused primarily on the best wireless headphones for this guide. While wired headphones have their fans, wireless headphones are just more convenient for most of us, though some of us are also fans of Apple's EarPods. With the release of the new noise-cancelling wired earbuds from Bose, we will be keeping our testing pool open to more wired models and will update this guide accordingly, should any earn a spot.

Most recently, we tested the Marshall Monitor III, JBL Tour One M3 headphones, and the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC, and though they had their merits, they fell short of winning the best of the best spot on this guide.

We've also tested the Sonos Ace headphones and Dyson OnTrac headphones. And while we loved them both for sound quality and noise cancellation, they fare in the way of AirPods Max — left out of our recommendations for their high price points.

August 2026: Following the release of the second generation Bose QuietComfort headphones, we've added them to our list as the best budget pick from Bose for headphones.

March 2025: We've designated the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 earbuds as the most comfortable ANC earbuds and crowned the Sony XM6 earbuds as the new best noise-cancelling earbuds.

December 2025: We replaced the Jabra Elite 8 Active Gen 2 earbuds, which are no longer available, with the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 sports earbuds.

December 2025: We removed the Marshall Mode wired earbuds, as they're frequently out of stock.

December 2025: We added the Sony WH-CH720N Noise-Canceling Headphones as the best headphones under $100.

December 2025: We added the Sony XM5 headphones, originally released in 2022, as our new honorable mention pick.

August 2026: We replaced the Sennheiser Momentum 4 with the Nothing Headphone (a) as our best battery life pick.

A few major headphone releases happened in September: Sony's mid-range WH-10000XM4C headphones, Sony's budget WH-CH730N headphones, and the Beats 360, the first pair of over-ear headphones from the brand in three years. From Bose, we've also recently seen new wired noise-cancelling earbuds, as well as two new pairs of open earbuds. We'll be comparing them against our current picks to see if they have a spot among our favorites.

No, we didn't forget to include the iconic Apple AirPods Max in our guide to the best headphones. It's not that we don't like them — in fact, we think they sound and look great (emphasis on look). However, after testing and re-testing them, we think they're just too expensive to justify a wholehearted recommendation. While we appreciate that they now (finally) come with lossless audio, they're still behind on features like battery life.

While they're still a smart choice for style-conscious Apple fans, we can no longer include them among the elite. We thought they were way too expensive upon their initial release, and we only feel more firm in this position six years later.

While the long-anticipated AirPods Max 2 are finally out, our reviewer found the upgrades to be minimal. At the same $549 the original Maxes were released at, these headphones are just too expensive and underperforming for us to recommend them.

Like with most products, this comes down to personal preference, but there are a few brands known for making really solid headphones. For those who appreciate quality ANC above all else, Bose headphones will be the best brand. Enjoy a rich and balanced sound profile? You'll want to check out Sony. In the budget space, Anker Soundcore products have impressed us lately. Still, we recommend reading each of our above picks to see which speaks most to you.

If you're wondering what headphones you've been seeing all over your For You page, it's likely a pair of Sonys, either the older WH-1000XM5s or the brand new Sony WH-1000XM6s. The former two used to be our top picks, but the XM6s now take the crown. Beats headphones are also incredibly popular, especially as brands like Marshall and Jabra fall out of favor.

Other than those, the Bose QuietComfort line is a popular pick, especially for those who wear their headphones for long periods of time. And of course, Apple AirPods are a popular pick for iPhone users who prefer earbuds over headphones. We're not huge fans of the AirPods Max, though, as we think they're too overpriced for what they offer. However, with Apple's recent updates to the AirPods line, we know they are top of mind.

Every single pair of headphones we included in this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. You can learn about our in-depth process by taking a look at the standardized testing guide we developed for this category.

Below, you'll find our condensed testing criteria for headphones:

We listened to a wide variety of genres of music, podcasts, and other forms of media. If a pair didn't at least sound solid across the board, they didn't make our list. In this category, we also considered the quality (and existence) of any equalizers.

We'll test ANC power around our homes as we work, with and without an audio assist, and outdoors. If headphones have customizable ANC levels, or automatic switching between noise-cancelling modes, we make sure that they actually provide noticeable differences in performance.

Everything from comfort to touch controls fall under this category. We look at what headphones offer to provide the best wear for the greatest amount of people, whether that be a strong selection of earbud tip sizes or particularly soft padding. Whenever possible, we test and re-test headphones over longer periods of time to see how they hold up.

We evaluate how headphones perform in all of the above categories, and if that performance matches their price point.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for three years at Mashable.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#484. Restaurant Brands reports mixed results as Burger King's U.S. turnaround shows signs of success

Restaurant Brands International on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as Popeyes' struggles offset Burger King's successful U.S. turnaround.

Shares of the company fell about 2% in morning trading.

Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Restaurant Brands reported third-quarter net income attributable to common shareholders of $542 million, or $1.54 per share, up from $315 million, or 96 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding certain noncash items, the company earned $1.10 per share.

Across all of its restaurants, the company reported same-store sales growth of 3.8%. Restaurant Brands has reported same-store sales growth above 3% for the past five quarters.

While the broader industry saw traffic soften in the third quarter as gas prices stayed high, Restaurant Brands said it has not seen any significant changes in consumer behavior.

"The environment, from what we see, has been relatively stable over the last couple of quarters and even into recent months," Restaurant Brands CEO Josh Kobza told CNBC.

Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. The burger chain's home market is in the middle of multiyear turnaround, with a focus on improving its food and restaurants.

"The plans we've put in place over the last several years are working, and we're going to keep executing against them," Restaurant Brands Chair Patrick Doyle said on the company's earnings conference call. "Burger King has delivered over four years of industry outperformance, and now we've seen three consecutive quarters of truly exceptional results."

After improving the quality of its Whopper earlier this year, Burger King turned its attention to its nuggets and sauces.

"Nuggets and sauces, frankly, we knew for a while that there was an opportunity," Kobza told CNBC. "We've heard it loud and clear from our guests."

Since Burger King relaunched its nuggets on Sept. 1, with 100% white meat chicken, sales have shot up more than 35%, Kobza said on the earnings call. More core menu items will get an upgrade next year.

Tim Hortons reported same-store sales growth of 1.8% in Canada, its home market. In July, the coffee chain launched a line of matcha drinks, bringing more customers to its locations during the sleepier afternoon hours.

Popeyes was once again the laggard of Restaurant Brands' portfolio. The fried chicken chain's U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%.

In recent quarters, Popeyes has struggled as other chicken rivals have lured its customers away with discounts. Restaurant Brands is trying to stage a comeback with improved restaurant operations and a focus on its core menu.

Restaurant Brands previously forecast that Popeyes would return to same-store sales growth in the second half of 2026, but Kobza said on the earnings call that the company now believes it will take longer, although traffic is improving. The return of Popeyes' $6 Big Box promotion in September boosted sales less than expected, according to Kobza. Plus, the chain has scaled back its wings to refocus on its core menu items, hurting sales in the short term.

The company's international business saw same-store sales growth of 3.9%, fueled by its Burger King locations.

#483. Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches

Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that,"  coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.

#481. The 6 best budget headphones of the year are all under $100

If you want to cheat the system a bit and get your hands on incredible, crisp sound from a pair of headphones under $100, we've got you. You no longer need to choose between a cheap pair of headphones and incredible features like active noise cancellation, Hi-Res Audio certification, and multi-device pairing.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Sure, you might have your eyes on the class-leading Sony WH-1000xM6 headphones, but they'll cost you $450. It's not necessary to dish out that much money when you can get headphones for a fraction of the price (with much of the same functionality) or, better yet, noise-cancelling headphones that carry longer battery life and a stronger sonic punch than the AirPods Max.

All this to say, cheap headphones can be genuinely great headphones — if you know where to look. That's why we've tested a bunch of picks under $100 to find the best budget headphones available. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

If you're still an Apple loyalist when it comes to headphones, stick with us for a sec. You'll soon discover that these top picks from popular budget audio brands like JLab, Anker, and JBL are giving the market’s best a run for their money. We even have a bargain entry from Sony that’s well worth a look.

Don't believe it? You'll want to see for yourself by reading our reviews of the best headphones under $100 below.

It's hard to find a better value pair of headphones than the JLab JBuds Lux ANC, especially on sale. During Black Friday 2025, we saw them drop all the way down to $27.99, but we've also caught them on sale just under $40 and $50 year-round. For balanced sound and adjustable ANC, that's an absolute steal.

Lead Shopping Reporter Bethany Allard tried out these headphones and came away with the take that they're the Bose QuietComfort headphones made affordable. Their sound profile is relatively balanced out of the box, but even better after some adjusting with the equalizer in the app. The ANC is solid, especially for their price point, and with the app, can also be adjusted to different levels (which isn't even a given on more premium headphones like the QuietComforts).

Their design also invokes the more expensive headphones, offering a standard look in a nice array of colorways. Senior Shopping Reporter Haley Henschel owns these headphones herself and especially appreciates the long-wear comfort they provide (Allard found them a little uncomfortable after a few hours of wear, so this can vary from person to person). Still, undeniably, their 40-hour battery life also allows for extended wear time, making them an especially great option for anyone who travels frequently or likes to wear over-ear headphones while they work.

Retailing at $49.95, the price tag on these JBL Tune 510BT headphones is kind of unbeatable, making them ideal for those who are trying to save money. Don't expect them to perform magical acts for you, but also don't underestimate this handy JBL pair. They're great if you're not devoted enough of an audiophile to consider professional-level sound quality (or lack thereof) a dealbreaker.

The Tune 510BT headphones do everything wireless headphones are supposed to: They provide reasonably good sound quality, allow you to switch between two device audio outputs at once, and last for days on end. Each of these points comes with a caveat — to be expected when your headphones come out costing less than 50 bucks.

As for sound quality, these JBLs won't provide active noise cancellation (though their ear cups certainly protect your ears from hearing what goes on in the outside environment). That being said, you'll still hear a bit of outside noise mixed with your favorite song.

When testing out the multi-device connection of this JBL model, we found that it was possible but worked in a much slower fashion than its counterparts. In other words, when stopping a video on YouTube and immediately launching into a song on the phone, the headphones didn't immediately reflect this switch: It took them a good three to four seconds to start playing the second audio input.

In terms of battery life, we were impressed with the fact that these headphones were fully drained only after 38 hours — which comes quite close to JBL's promise of a 40-hour battery life. The device gave off a little tone that signified the battery was almost out, but this feature (in a real-life versus for-testing-only setting) is honestly "too little, too late." Unlike in other headphone models, there unfortunately wasn't a voice that announced the exact battery percentage when powering on the Tune 510BTs. To make up for this small flaw, the headphones are equipped with Quick Charge functionality. Just five minutes of them being plugged in via a USB-C connection adds two hours of power. Pretty sweet.

These headphones are massive — reminiscent of a gaming headset (think wide and deep ear cups, a thick band, and an undeniable heaviness). That being said, they certainly aren’t meant for working out (especially not running), unless you don't mind wearing something clunky and heavy on your head while boosting those endorphins. If you're planning on wearing them around the house, on a long plane ride, or during your daily gaming ritual, you'll fall in love with these budget headphones. After all, nothing about them screams "budget" and they're super new on the market.

Despite their cumbersome frame, these headphones take “accommodation” to the next level with a floating axis design, rotating ear cups, and a cozy plush headband.

The Space One outclass their rivals in two key areas. The first is (and don't laugh) the fact that they come with a cute, color-coordinated carrying bag. The second is that five quick minutes of charging boosts the power of these headphones not by one hour, not by two hours, but by four whole hours. They also have three mics with an AI algorithm that pinpoints your voice and amplifies it on calls. In case you don't want to hear the voices of others, they are specially designed to reduce crowd noise by up to 98 percent.

In terms of how this crowd noise reduction feature fared in real-time, I would say that the passive noise cancellation aspect of the headphones was more responsible for making it feel like you're in your own musical bubble than the ANC. We still recommend trying the adaptive noise cancellation feature since it adequately adjusts noise reduction to your surroundings. You’ll get to enjoy the full-bodied sound that blasts from Anker’s 40mm dynamic drivers with minimal interference.

The (completely free) Soundcore app is chock-full of add-on features that you can enable at your convenience. One of these is currently in beta testing — it's called Easy Chat and lowers your music volume when it detects speech. While this is theoretically good for calls (no more scrambling to turn off your rap/hip-hop song queue when grandma calls to check in), I once started to sing along to a song, which sadly turned off, thanks to this feature being enabled. Bear that in mind when toying with all of Soundcore's fancy audio tools.

If you don't need all the bells and whistles that come with top-of-the-line headphones, the Sony WH-CH520 will likely check your must-have boxes. To be completely frank, these Sonys look akin to headsets given out on flights — what with their primitive earpads, basic head cushion band, and inability to completely fold into themselves to save space. Yet, functionality sometimes trumps appearances, and this sentiment rings true for the WH-CH520 model.

Sony's WH-CH520 headphones are a great pair of affordable, basic headphones. They'd be nice for working out or sitting in the office. And they come in stylish colors like butter yellow and pink.

Through the compatible Sony app, you can manage connected devices, play around with the sound equalizer, set up "360 Reality Audio" by analyzing your ear shape, and choose whether you want to prioritize sound quality or stable connection. The learning curve to figuring out the headphones' on-ear controls is not steep at all: Press the "+" button twice to skip forward a song, the "-" button twice to go back, and the power button to start or stop.

Beware — the headphones' ear cups are kind of tiny, which can provide an uncomfortable experience for those whose ears are on the larger side. They're meant to sit on top of your ears, rather than enclose them like over-ear headphones. As far as durability goes, we could only infer that snapping the headphones' band in two would be an easy task, since this pair felt quite flimsy overall and wasn't all too cushioned. Still, the audio quality of this Sony pair certainly packed a punch. When running in them (pretty comfortable, all things considered), the sound of traffic and the wind was just barely audible — certainly way less audible than you'd expect from such a minimalistic headphone design.

Sometimes you just want headphones that require very little charging when necessary, and the Wave Pro fit that description to a T. We’re talking nearly three times the amount of battery life as the market’s top-selling models, plus some of the strongest quick charging available. Not to mention, they sound great.

Other models on this list may provide longer charges, but the Wave Pro have the most accurate battery life ratings. A full charge generates between 50 to 55 hours of noise-cancelling use and 75 to 80 hours when disabling the feature. Our unit averages a recharge once a month.

The combination of 40mm DLC dynamic drivers, Hi-Res Audio certification, and LDAC creates resonant sound that streams at three times the bitrate of standard codecs. Bass is robust on contemporary tracks, while vocals are striking on ballads and live performances. EarFun’s adjustable 10-band EQ leaves room to tweak the soundstage to your liking, though it’s best to stick with the default settings. Turning on ANC will tune out a high number of disruptive sounds. Music sounds just as good in ambient mode; you can hear what’s happening in proximity loudly and clearly, and it won’t affect playback.

Design-wise, the Wave Pro are constructed better than, I'd say, 90 percent of similarly priced competitors. Their all-plastic frame with plush leather earpads and headband supplies enough comfort and protection for long-term use.

Even if the call quality and controls leave much to be desired, the Wave Pro make up for these shortcomings with their prominent hallmarks.

We highly recommend the Major IV to brand enthusiasts who love Marshall’s legacy audio and minimalist retro aesthetic. Those are two heritage traits that the brand always knocks out of the park, and this modern wireless audio release is no different.

Besides their markdown in price (down to $100 from $150), the Major IV put on an audio clinic. These headphones sound articulate, clean, and engaging. Depth and nuance are noticeable from the moment you press play. There is no need for sound customization, which is great considering the headphones lack the settings to do so.

Marshall’s ingenuity is well demonstrated through its physical controls. Look at the gold-plated multi-directional knob that allows for seamless operation (call management, device pairing, playback, voice activation). Its solid tactility ensures that users' intended commands are met. The other feature that gives these old school-looking cans some ultramodern swagger is wireless charging. Say what? Yes, these headphones work with Qi-compatible chargers to power up without being tethered to a USB-C cable. I have not seen this on any other pair of headphones. Up to 80 hours of playtime is another major selling point.

Complaints can be made about the Major IV’s discomfort and poor noise isolation. Those are the compromises you’ll have to deal with for professional sound performance.

Check out our review of the updated Marshall Major V.

In case we weren't clear enough before, cheaper does not mean worse by any means (and vice versa) when it comes to headphones. Not always, at least.

Yet, the general trend still stands that the "higher-end" a pair of headphones is, the more likely you are to get better sound quality (aka undistorted bass), more playtime, and state-of-the-art features like adaptive ANC.

Budget headphones are known to leak sound more often than their pricier alternatives, and they'll likely have fewer extras, like spatial audio for immersive 3D sound and TalkThru technology (which amplifies your convo buddy's voice while reducing music volume instantly) featured in some of JBL’s flagship headphones.

Nonetheless, we made it our mission to find headphones — both on-ear and over-ear models — that aren't "higher-end" in price and borrow a lot of standout functionality from their more expensive counterparts.

The simple-and-sweet answer to this question is "Bluetooth." When you don't want dangling wires interfering with your music listening experience (unless you're a TikTok girly who wants to intentionally flaunt the wires on walks), Bluetooth comes in to save the day — by providing your headphones with seamless cross-device compatibility. According to PCMag, "wireless no longer means poor sound and battery life." Bluetooth headphones "still compress hi-res audio, but... preserve quality much better than in the past, and battery life has steadily improved with each new generation." Upon setting up your newest headphones purchase, you'll be prompted to connect to a device via Bluetooth. The whole process should only take you about 5 seconds. Simplicity, after all, is key.

Think of it as the real-life definition of "headphones on, world off." Active noise cancellation achieves the effect of tuning out your surroundings by using mics that capture exterior noises. Then, "audio processing circuitry... takes those noises and generates their inverse to cancel them out in real-time," as PCMag explained.

PS: There's also something called passive noise cancellation. It uses physical engineering to manually insulate your ears. Most earbuds and over-ear headphones already have this kind of noise cancellation handy — arising from the sheer shape of the earplug tips that fit snugly into your ear or the way over-ear cups create a seal that blocks off extraneous sound.

Not all of the headphones we tested boast ANC, but those that do allow you to turn on what's called transparency mode, which is a fancy way of saying you'll be able to hear your surroundings if you choose. Sometimes, you can even manipulate just how much of the outside world you want within (literal) earshot. This feature proves super helpful for city dwellers who don't want to get hit by a car while blasting "Empire State of Mind" at full volume.

To bring you this list of the very best under-$100 wireless headphones, we rigorously tested headphones over three to four weeks. While testing, we considered:

The selections on this lift were driven first by price, as we wanted the options here to be truly affordable. Everything on this list is under $100, and we tested if the value matched the price.

We tested these earbuds with various songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls.

This variable revolved around the aesthetic feel of each tested item, how comfortable it was during wear, and how well it was able to withstand daily use. We assessed whether their features translated to unnecessary bulk and whether they were travel-friendly (could fold into a tight bundle, came with a case, etc.).

With wireless headphones, you have to rely on a battery charge, so we considered which headphones will last multiple wears without needing recharged.

#471. European Central Bank (ECB) head Christine Lagarde to step down in February, before her term ends

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde is to resign nine months ahead of the end of her 8-year term. European Council President Antonio Costa has said the process to find a successor is underway.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the European Central Bank for seven years, has announced that she is stepping down prematurely from the position.

"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.

European Council President Antonio Costa said a process to find her successor would start immediately.

The announcement comes ahead of a key meeting of the bank this week that is likely to focus on France's deteriorating public finances.

No reason has so far been given for Lagarde's premature departure, but there has been speculation that she would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose her successor before French elections in the spring that could see a eurosceptic far-right victory influence the choice.

Her term, which began on November 1, 2019, would normally have ended at the end of October 2027.

Lagarde, a former French finance minister, was also head of the International Monetary Fund from 2011 to 2019.

Costa praised Lagarde's leadership during her seven-year stint at the ECB helm, a period in which the EU and the world faced great challenges.

"Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa posted on social media.

"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision," Costa said.

Lagarde herself has voiced satisfaction with her record.

"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde, a French economist, said in a short video shared on ​social media.

The ECB head is chosen by the leaders of the 21 eurozone countries.

The announcement of Lagarde's imminent departure comes as the ECB is to hold a meeting this week where it is expected to keep its ​deposit rate at 2.5%, while signaling that this is likely to rise again before the end of the year.

The bank has already raised interest rates twice since June in a bid to curb inflation fueled by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.

However, Thursday's meeting is also likely to focus on the fiscal and political crisis in France, Europe's second-biggest economy.

French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, rose to their highest level in 25 years last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget.

Recent protests, at which many demonstrators were calling for more spending on public services, were also marred by considerable violence.

There has been speculation as to whether the ECB could, for the first time, use the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI),  a crisis-fighting tool that allows the bank to buy bonds of a eurozone member if yields rise uncontrollably and there is a risk of financial stress spreading.

However, most observers believe the problems in France do not yet meet the strict conditions stipulated for its use.

#470. Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise

Shares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings surged 13% Thursday after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its outlook for the full year.

The cruise line reported third-quarter revenue of $2.95 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $2.88 billion, according to analyst estimates from LSEG.

Net income for the period was $491 million, or $1.07 per share.

Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $937 million, which exceeded Norwegian's previous guidance of $874 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.12, exceeding previous guidance of 90 cents and outpacing analysts' expectations of 94 cents, per LSEG.

Norwegian also raised its full-year guidance, citing its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance. The company now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $2.55 billion and adjusted EPS of about $1.70.

The report said the company's bookings had "improved modestly" since its last report but remain below its optimal range.

Norwegian said it will emphasize new marketing strategies, including the launch of a new marketing platform in January. It also said it anticipates that enhancements such as a new waterpark at its Great Stirrup Cay private island will support stronger demand.

Also on Thursday, Norwegian announced that Chief Financial Officer Mark Kempa will step down after more than 25 years at the company. Meghan Montana, currently chief strategy officer, will take over the role starting Jan. 1.

#465. Merck tops quarterly estimates, hikes profit outlook as new Keytruda form shows strength

Merck on Thursday topped third-quarter estimates and hiked its adjusted profit outlook, as its immunotherapy Keytruda, including a newer injectable form of the drug, showed stronger-than-expected sales.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects adjusted earnings to be between $2.77 and $2.82 per share. That adjusted profit outlook is up from a previous range of $2.66 to $2.76 per share. The guidance now includes a one-time charge of $400 million, or 12 cents per share, related to its licensing agreement with the Chinese cancer drugmaker SciBrunch.

Merck also narrowed the low end of its 2026 revenue guidance, now expecting sales between $66.8 billion and $67.3 billion. That compares to a previous outlook of $66.3 billion to $67.3 billion.

The company has been on a deal spree as it races to offset generic competition for Keytruda after key patents begin expiring in 2028.

Merck is also positioning the new form of the drug, Keytruda Qlex, as a cornerstone of its growth strategy. The goal is to transition patients from the original intravenous version to Qlex, considered a more convenient under-the-skin injection. This strategy allows the company to defend its market share and sustain Keytruda's blockbuster sales beyond the original version's loss of exclusivity.

Keytruda raked in $8.60 billion in sales for the quarter, beating the $7.73 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That includes $830 million in sales for Qlex – the highest seen in a quarter since it launched in 2025.

Analysts were expecting $649 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates said. The blowout quarter for the shot suggests it could soon eventually be a multibillion-dollar product annually.

Here's what Merck reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

The company posted a net income of $5.07 billion, or $2.04 per share, for the quarter. That compares with net income of $5.79 billion, or $2.32 per share, for the year-earlier period.

Excluding acquisition and restructuring costs, Merck posted earnings of $2.49 per share for the third quarter.

Merck raked in $18.09 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 5% from the same period a year earlier.

Beyond Keytruda, Merck's newer products also showed strong growth.

Winrevair, which is used to treat a rare, deadly lung condition, generated $694 million in sales for the quarter, up 93% from the same period a year earlier. Analysts were expecting sales of $645 million.

Meanwhile, the Gardasil vaccine, which prevents cancers from HPV, a very common sexually transmitted infection, drew about $2 billion in sales due to higher demand in the U.S. That tops the $1.76 billion in sales that analysts were expecting.

That strong revenue comes after Merck last year grappled with elevated Gardasil inventory and weak demand for the vaccine in China.

Meanwhile, Merck's animal health business posted $1.68 billion in sales for the third quarter, which came in slightly below analysts' estimates.

#464. Election Day 2026: Find when polls open, close, and other voting details

The Nov. 3 midterm elections are here, and the outcome will determine the makeup of Congress and the trajectory of President Donald Trump's remaining years in office.

So if you haven't already voted, still need to mail in a ballot, or don't even know where to start, the hours are counting down. For an overview of voting deadlines, drop box and polling locations, and registration information, visit Vote.org, USA.gov, or keep reading below.

More than 51 million Americans have already voted in the 2026 midterm elections. The number of people voting by mail grew substantially in 2020, and eight states now host what are known as all-mail elections or offer universal mail-in voting.

Mail ballots are sent early, with most states requiring at least a week's lead time before Nov. 3. If you were issued an absentee or mail ballot and plan to send it by mail, your ballot must be postmarked by or on election day, not after. A late postmark can void your ballot. If you never received your ballot, contact your election office ASAP.

In some states, voters can also drop off their ballots at designated drop boxes (the websites of county registrars typically list drop box locations, such as the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder). Around 15 states require drop box options for voters, many located at places like libraries and parks:

Another 11 states prohibit drop boxes, so make sure your ballot gets postmarked if you are registered in these states:

To find more rules on drop box voting, absentee voting, and voting by mail, visit your state's registrar of voters or scroll down to the state-by-state database on Vote.org.

Despite a growing number of voters skipping the polls in favor of mail, many voters still cast their ballot in person. Voters are assigned to an in-person polling location based on the address they used to register to vote, and most can start voting before Nov. 3.

Polling times vary by state, with some states offering in-person voting as early as one month before election day (this practice is usually referred to as early in-person voting). Voters with disabilities may need to go to a different polling location, depending on their accommodation needs.

Voters do not need any special equipment or documents to cast their vote. You may need to bring a form of verification to the polls, however, depending on your state. Scroll down for more information.

Voters are also allowed to bring in personal notes, a voter's guide, and even sample ballots into the polling booth.

Voters can find out their nearest polling location by checking their registration or calling their local registrar of voters. They can also use an online polling locator such Vote.org or the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS).

That depends on your state. Voter ID laws vary across the country, so check with your state election officials to be sure. In some cases, you may still be able to vote without an ID by signing an identity form.

Can I track my ballot if I voted by mail?

Yes. Most states offer some form of ballot tracking for voters. Find specific information on ballot tracking via your state's registrar website or call 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683).

Yes and no. Ballots can't be challenged without a real legal basis under the National Voter Registration Act. A voter purge, in which election workers "clean up" voter databases by deleting names, can't be conducted within 90 days of a federal election. If you were on the roll as of August, filled out your ballot correctly and on time, your vote should count.

Federal agents and law enforcement cannot legally seize voting machines, nullify ballots, or stop the count.

That being said, groups may still challenge swaths of ballots up until the election. If your registration is challenged at the polls, you can still cast a provisional ballot.

Electronic voting apparatuses are overseen by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC) and thousands of election officials to ensure their safety and reliability. While recent studies have uncovered security flaws, election security researchers say they have not yet led to any kind of election interference, as suggested by some critics and conspiracy theorists.

Instead, experts suggest the biggest threat to election integrity is the spread of misinformation, which is increasingly enabled by AI.

Can the president intervene in the election?

The administration has been casting doubt on the legitimacy of the midterm results, including claims that thousands of noncitizens are casting votes in this year's election. The majority of noncitizen voters charged with crimes have been found to be lawful residents.

Despite threats from the Trump administration, the president cannot issue an executive order or harness emergency powers to take over or nationalize the election process. Previous executive orders attempting to change the electoral process have been struck down or blocked by courts, and additional safeguards prevent the current Congress from refusing to seat newly elected officials.

Chase joined Mashable's Social Good team in 2020, covering online stories about digital activism, climate justice, accessibility, and media representation. Her work also captures how these conversations manifest in politics, popular culture, and fandom. Sometimes she's very funny.

#463. Germany news: Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses North Korea of threatening Europe's freedom

Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said North Korea is putting Europe's security at risk by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in Ukraine. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026.

The biggest news story out of Germany this evening had to do with the Left candidate Elif Eralp having sparked controversy with internal remarks to Der Spiegel.

A German news magazine's decision to publish private interview notes has sparked a controversy surrounding Berlin's potential next mayor.

On Thursday, Der Spiegel published internal comments on an interview by Elif Eralp, who led the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) to victory in September's state election. Her office had accidentally included the remarks while approving an interview for publication.

In the notes, Eralp expressed fears for her family's safety if she publicly named Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian activist who is reported to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which the EU designates a terrorist organization. Ibrahim had attended the Left Party's election-night celebrations and was photographed with prominent Left Party Bundestag member Ferat Koçak.

Eralp also cited advice she received from Berlin police against publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime, though that advice was reportedly related to a separate case. Der Spiegel questioned whether her fears could affect her independence as mayor. Eralp rejected suggestions that she could be intimidated and pledged firm action against terrorism and organized crime.

The timing is significant. Eralp, the daughter of Turkish immigrants, could become Berlin's first Left Party mayor and the first woman of Turkish descent to hold the office. Her party won 25.7% of the vote in September's election and hopes to form a government with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Both prospective partners have approved formal coalition negotiations.

The Left must decide whether to follow suit at a party conference this Saturday, October 31. The far-left party is also facing accusations of antisemitism involving some of its members. Newly elected lawmaker Vanessa Emde faces possible exclusion from the Left's parliamentary group following comments questioning whether states, including Israel, have an inherent right to exist. The Left has been part of Berlin coalition governments before but has never led one. The controversy comes at a pivotal moment in its effort to do so.

Germany's leaders are on a foreign relations push, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a trip to South Korea, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Panama and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in China.

Merz spoke of the threat North Korea posed to Europe's freedom by supplying troops to fight in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He wraps up his visit with a trip to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, meanwhile, is in Panama where he is visiting ahead of traveling to Atlanta for the G20 meeting.

Wadephul is there to promote free trade and also handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.

And then German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities in China and picked up a ping-pong paddle for a game with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll, who is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul landed in Panama on Wednesday evening for a visit.

After his arrival at Panama City airport, Wadephul handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.

The aid shipment is made up of about 20 tons of supplies. Panama was hit by a powerful earthquake earlier this month.

The supplies include water filters, blankets, tarpaulins, cots and kitchen sets worth over €150,000 ($167,000).

More than 5,000 people are still being housed in emergency shelters, weeks after the magnitude-7.7 quake on October 9, which resulted in injuries and damaged hundreds of buildings.

Wadephul also thanked the Central American country for maintaining the Panama Canal "so responsibly and ensuring it is fit for the future, as well as more generally focusing on preserving balance in the region."

Restrictions on other sea routes due to the conflict in the Middle East has meant that the Panama Canal is more important to global trade than ever.

Wadephul is due to hold talks on Thursday with Martinez-Acha Vasquez and President Jose Raul Mulino.

Wadephul will travel to the US state of Georgia for the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday.

Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.

After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.

In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.

Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.

He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.

To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.

Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.

Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.

Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."

The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."

But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."

"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.

"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.

Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.

This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."

He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.

According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.

"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.

Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.

On the final day of his state visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership and hold talks with, among others, President Xi Jinping.

Steinmeier is making his first visit to China in eight years, as he seeks to boost bilateral ties.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday said North Korea was threatening "freedom throughout Europe" by sending soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine.

After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Merz highlighted that Russia was supplying weapons to North Korea.

The chancellor said this arrangement therefore shows how "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects Korea's security."

North Korea has boosted its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Pyongyang has provided Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. It has also, according to South Korean intelligence services, sent about 15,000 soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces.

In exchange, Russia provides financial backing, military technology and security guarantees to North Korea.

Before Merz's arrival on Thursday, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, according to the South Korean military.

At the start of his visit, Merz said he hoped that Korea would eventually be unified. The peninsula has been split along the 38th parallel since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953.

Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen their two nations' strategic and security ties, which includes joint military exercises and exchange of intelligence.

The chancellor is expected to conclude his trip to South Korea with a visit to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.

Germany is looking for new partners in Asia. As Chancellor Friedrich Merz travels to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, Berlin is trying to reduce its economic dependence on China while adapting to a changing global order. But can countries in the Indo-Pacific, besides China, help Germany diversify its trade and security partnerships?

This week on Berlin Briefing, DW's Giulia Saudelli speaks with DW Business Reporter Steven Beardsley and DW Chief Political Correspondent Nina Haase, who is traveling with the chancellor.

The South Korean leader made the announcement after a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Seoul.

The two leaders also agreed ​to ⁠improve bilateral ties to ⁠an "enhanced ​strategic partnership," Lee said.

An eight-year-old girl sustained serious injuries after she was attacked by at least one wolf at a wildlife park in Brandenburg in east Germany.

The child was brought to hospital by a rescue helicopter on Wednesday.

Local officials said a zookeeper had helped prevent other children from being attacked.

Police are investigating how and why the attack occurred, which took place during a special program for children.

Police on Thursday said their investigation was centered on a staff member who was in the enclosure with the children, a spokeswoman said.

The Teltow-Fläming district administration said the incident happened before the wildlife park's regular opening hours as part of an "Animal Keeper Day" for children.

The administration also said the attack had taken place in the polar wolf enclosure.

"While the animals in the wildlife enclosure were being watered, the wolves kept there attacked a girl and seriously injured her," the district administration said.

The zookeeper's quick action prevented "further harm to two other girls" who were also at the scene, the district added.

The park will remain closed for the time being, officials said, as authorities launch a safety review at the wildlife park, which is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin.

Police are still probing the circumstances that led to the children being inside the enclosure.

The Johannismühle Wildlife Park said it was cooperating with authorities but could not provide further details due to the open investigation.

"We deeply regret the incident, and the affected family has our full support," the park said.

The wildlife park was closed until further notice "due to technical reasons," a sign at the entrance said on Thursday.

A wolf bit a woman in a busy shopping area in Hamburg this year, in what is thought to be the first such attack since wolves were reintroduced to the country in 1998.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is visiting Seoul, said at the start of his visit that he hopes North and South Korea will eventually be reunited.

The Korean Peninsula has been divided into two states since the Korean War ended in 1953.

Merz pointed to his own country's division between West and East Germany for much of the second half of the 20th century.

"Korea and Germany are united by the painful experience of division," he wrote in the guest book during his meeting with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

"I also wish for the people of Korea what we are fortunate to experience in Germany: unity in freedom."

North Korea is a largely isolated dictatorship ruled by Kim Jong Un, while the South is a democracy that has close ties with the West.

Merz is set to visit the demilitarized zone (DMZ), which divides the two countries, on Friday.

Volkswagen (VW) reported third quarter losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) on Thursday, as it faces rising competition from China.

Germany's biggest car maker had reported a loss of just over €1.07 billion in the same period last year.

Volkswagen, like other car makers, has struggled to keep pace with fierce competition from China, the world's biggest car market. VW has also struggled with the transition to electric vehicles and with declining demand.

Volkswagen last month warned that its 10-brand group, which includes makers such as Audi, Seat and Skoda, was facing a 10-billion-euro hit to its annual profits.

The most significant hit came from Porsche, Volkswagen's luxury sports car and SUV subsidiary. Porsche, which was once a major driver of profits for the VW group, was also one of the main factors behind VW's quarterly losses in 2025.

The luxury brand has been hit by a sales slump in China, US tariff policy and its electric vehicle strategy.

VW announced this year that it plans to cut over 100,000 jobs across the group by the end of the decade as it tries to reduce costs. It announced on Thursday that its restructuring would cost the company 31 billion euros.

The company is considering or has decided to shut down multiple German factories — including plants in Zwickau, Emden, Hanover, and Neckarsulm.

"What matters now is swift and consistent implementation," Arno Antlitz, VW's chief financial officer said in a statement. "We cannot lose any time and need to act quickly and decisively."
